title: Milestone: Two Families of Faith
objective: After this level you can compare the Abrahamic and Indian traditions: one life and a final judgment, or many lives and release from rebirth.
summary: Traditional Judaism, Christianity and Islam look to one lifetime, resurrection and a Last Judgment; the Indian family sees many lives, karma and release.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Two families of faith, one big question.
cards.body: What comes after this life? Level 8 sorted religions into families. Now, with Hindus and Jains met up close, set the Abrahamic and Indian families side by side and watch their answers diverge.

items.label: Abrahamic family
points: Traditionally one lifetime, then resurrection and a Last Judgment

items.label: Indian family
points: Many lives in samsara, shaped by karma
The hope is release (moksha) from rebirth
Time turns in cycles of destruction and renewal

cards.headline: Many voices on each side
cards.body: Neither side is one voice. Muslims believe in a Day of Judgement, when every human life will be assessed. The Catholic Church teaches that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead. Maimonides counted resurrection of the dead among his 13 principles of Jewish faith, though Jews have long debated it. In both families your actions reach beyond this life: weighed at a final judgment, or carried forward by karma.

cards.headline: Milestone: two families compared
learned: How scholars describe any faith fairly, bracketing the question of truth.
What Jews believe God promised Abraham, and how Judaism carried on after the Temple fell.
What Christians mean by the Trinity, and why Luther's Reformation split Western Christianity.
How the Five Pillars shape a Muslim's life, and why Sunnis and Shia first divided.
How karma and rebirth shape Hindu and Jain life, and how the Abrahamic faiths answer differently.

questions.prompt: Before comparing what Muslims and Hindus believe about the afterlife, a scholar "brackets" the question of truth. What does that mean?

options.label: Deciding first which of the two beliefs is correct
options.rationale: Bracketing sets that question aside; it doesn't answer it.

options.label: Comparing only the beliefs the two faiths share
options.rationale: Bracketing is about the scholar's judgment, not which beliefs to study.

options.label: Setting aside judgment to describe each faith fairly
Dropping the question of truth from religion for good
options.rationale: The question isn't thrown away, only set aside while describing.

questions.explanation: Bracketing (epoché) sets "is it true?" aside, so a believer and a skeptic could both accept the description.

questions.prompt: Why do Jewish families hold berit mila on a baby boy's eighth day?

options.label: It marks the covenant Jews believe God made with Abraham
It celebrates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai
options.rationale: Sinai is Moses' story; Genesis 17 ties this sign to Abraham.

options.label: It remembers the destruction of the Temple in 586 BCE
options.rationale: Tisha b'Av mourns the Temples; berit mila marks the covenant.

options.label: It marks a boy's coming of age as an adult in the faith
options.rationale: It happens in infancy, as the covenant's sign.

questions.explanation: Genesis 17 names circumcision the covenant's sign. In Judaism it represents the covenant between God and Abraham, marked again in each generation.

questions.prompt: Luther translated the Bible into German. Which of his principles did that put into practice?

options.label: Faith alone: salvation can't be earned by good works
options.rationale: That was his answer to indulgences; the translation served his other principle.

options.label: Obedience to the pope as the Bible's final interpreter
options.rationale: Luther challenged church authority and was excommunicated in 1521.

options.label: Nicaea's creed as the test of every church teaching
options.rationale: Luther's test was scripture itself.

options.label: Scripture alone: the Bible as the measure of teaching

questions.explanation: Sola scriptura made the Bible the measure of every church teaching; a German Bible let lay people read it without depending on church authority.

questions.prompt: When Muhammad died in 632, what did the groups that became Sunni and Shia disagree about?

options.label: Which verses belonged in the Quran
options.rationale: They shared the Quran.

options.label: Who should lead the community next
Whether Muhammad was the final prophet
options.rationale: Both hold that he was.

options.label: How many times a day Muslims should pray
options.rationale: The dispute was over leadership.

questions.explanation: Sunnis recognize Abu Bakr and the first four caliphs as rightful successors; Shia held that leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants.

questions.prompt: Why is ahimsa, non-violence, the heart of Jain teaching?

options.label: Jains believe harm angers a creator god who punishes it
options.rationale: The reason is souls and karma.

options.label: Every being has a soul, and harm binds karma to one's own
Ahimsa is a law passed by Mahavira's father
options.rationale: He left the palace; ahimsa is a teaching.

options.label: Jains avoid harm only on festival and fasting days
options.rationale: It shapes daily life.

questions.explanation: Every living thing has a soul, and harming others attracts karma, so protecting others protects your own soul.

questions.prompt: Which pairing matches each family's traditional view?

options.label: Abrahamic: many lives. Indian: one life and a final judgment
options.rationale: That's reversed.

options.label: Both: one lifetime followed by rebirth as an animal
options.rationale: Neither family teaches that.

options.label: Abrahamic: one lifetime and a Last Judgment. Indian: many lives and release
Both: time repeats in endless cycles
options.rationale: The Abrahamic view looks to an end of history.

questions.explanation: Traditional Judaism, Christianity and Islam hold to one lifetime and a Last Judgment; the Indian family sees samsara and hopes for release.

questions.prompt: A Muslim and a Hindu both believe actions matter beyond this life. How does each picture that?

options.label: Both expect actions to be weighed at the Day of Judgement
options.rationale: That is the Muslim picture.

options.label: Both expect karma to shape the body of their next birth
options.rationale: That is the Hindu picture.

options.label: Neither thinks their actions matter once this life ends
options.rationale: Both do, in different ways.

options.label: Muslim: one life judged. Hindu: karma carried into future lives

questions.explanation: A Day of Judgement is one of Islam's six articles of faith, when every life is assessed; many Hindus believe karma carries actions forward into lives to come.
